messages.subject: Abundance modeling with uneven pass numbers, two observers
parts:
Hello,

I have a couple questions on abundance modeling.  I’ve read through the past q and a, and had the chance to sit in on the first half of the webinar, but I’m new to all this and working through things. 

A quick rundown of what I have:  I conducted multi-pass snorkel surveys to count juvenile fish of one species. These passes were done by two different divers, surveying at different times, but within a short enough period to meet closure assumptions.  I'm only looking within one season. I'm interested in relationships between fish abundance and habitat, so I also collected habitat characteristics in each of the pools (eg. volume of wood, boulder density, etc.). Because of time and personnel limits, I wasn’t able to have an equal number of passes for all pools, leaving me with:

Site 1: 34 pools, all surveyed 5 times, 3x by diver 1, 2x by diver 2

Site 2: 43 pools, all surveyed 5 times, 3x by diver 1, 2x by diver 2

Site 3: 107 pools, 66% of pools surveyed once (all diver 1), 33% of pools surveyed 4 times (3x by diver 1, 1x by diver 2)

Site 4: 113 pools, 60% of pools surveyed once (all diver 1), 40% of pools surveyed 5 times (3x by diver 1, 2x by diver 2)

I’ve already taken site 1 through the steps of the pcount model, with 2 detection covariates (including which diver it was) and 3 abundance covariates based on the habitat data, and an offset of log(pool area) in the final model.  My observed counts range from around 10 to 120 or so, and I had some of the K-setting difficulty described in earlier posts.  The lambda estimate of the null poisson model stabilized around a K of 350, but the negative binomial null model was still changing past K=600, which is an unrealistic number for these systems.  Even with the full poisson model, the estimates for the counts seem too high, but at least everything seems to be running smoothly. 

My real questions lie with the rest of the data.  I’ve read that unmarked doesn’t have an option for random effects (here from the 4 different sites).  But maybe WinBugs does (I’ve never used it)?  Or I could run each site separately in unmarked.  The other trouble is the different number of passes of pools within a site.  Is it possible to include all the data (from an individual site) in the model, even if the numbers of passes are uneven across pools?  I tried using all the data lumped together, but came across an error during model specification (“Warning messages: 1: Some observations have been discarded because corresponding covariates were missing) and again when creating a fitList for selection (“Error in validityMethod(object) : Data are not the same among models due to missing covariate values. Consider removing NAs before analysis”).  Does this mean that unequal pass numbers within a data set are not allowed? 

Is there a better way to take care of the two-diver issue than using diver as a covariate for detection probability?

Any thoughts or suggestions would be much appreciated!

Kristen Kirkby

Graduate Research Assistant
Department of Fisheries and Wildlife
Oregon State University
kristen...@oregonstate.edu

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [SPAM]  [unmarked] Abundance modeling with uneven pass numbers, two observers
parts:
Hi Kristen,
 
unequal replication is no problem for the Nmix model. Using diver as a categorical covariate on detection appears a good idea. With only 4 sites, I would stack all data on top of each other and treat site as a fixed effect (yes, unmarked does not allow random effects, apart of course from the latent effects, for instance, the N's in each of your pools). What the warning messages mean is you can't compare your models in the FitList, because they are based on different data subsets. You can avoid this if you either throw out all rows of data that contain any missing covariate values. Or, if you only have few missing covariate values (e.g., less than 10%), consider "filling up" the covariates by mean imputation: replacing NAs with the covariate means.
 
If you get unrealistic abundance estimates then perhaps your system is not closed (i.e., temporary emigration) and you're estimating the superpopulation size. Also note that the NegBin mixture may sometimes yield unrealistically high abundance estimates; see also Johnson, Conservation Biology, ca. 2009.
 
Regards  --  Marc

messages.author: 681fb59733e01a1e
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Abundance modeling with uneven pass numbers, two observers
parts:
hi Kristen,
 
 You can definitely handle random effects of all sorts in WinBUGS and it shouldn't be too hard to implement that -- there are lots of examples out there (see Kery and Schaub's 2010 book).
 
 The unbalanced sampling should _not_ be a problem.  The y-matrix should have NA for the records. I think maybe if there is a corresponding NA for the covariate maybe pcount() is tossing out the whole record. I suggest putting any arbitrary value in for the covariate value and , I believe, that should have the desired effect.
 
 It sounds to me like your data suggest considerably over-disperson relative to the Poisson and in such cases it often works out that the Negative binomial model is unstable.   I'm not a big fan of that model and recommend sticking with the Poisson model and trying to model covariates or, as you suggested, random block effects of some sort.  I think the sensitivity of the NB estimates to varying K is a sufficient justification for falling back on the Poisson.
 Longer term, we need some better over-dispersion models in unmarked.  It would be nice to have a log-normal model and possibly others, but this isn't going to happen in the near term.
 
 Highly variable counts of the same site, when you're confident of "closure", could suggest variability in sampling conditions or, possibly, non-independence of detections due to, for example, schooling, or maybe density-dependence on detection probability. It would be worth trying to understand the underlying mechanisms and trying to model it explicitly.
 Marc Kery has been working on a type of non-independence model and he might be able to offer up an example in WinBUGS if you contact him directly.
 
regards,
andy

Hi Kristen,

The only thing I would add to what Marc and Andy said is that another option for handling NAs (so that you can compare models using AIC), is to add NAs to the y matrix that correspond to NAs in the covariates. This way you won't have to throw out an entire row of data, and you won't have to impute any data.

Richard

I’ve already taken site 1 through the steps of the pcount model, with 2 detection covariates (including which diver it was) and 3 abundance covariates based on the habitat data, and an offset of log(pool area) in the final model. My observed counts range from around 10 to 120 or so, and I had some of the K-setting difficulty described in earlier posts. The lambda estimate of the null poisson model stabilized around a K of 350, but the negative binomial null model was still changing past K=600, which is an unrealistic number for these systems. Even with the full poisson model, the estimates for the counts seem too high, but at least everything seems to be running smoothly.

My real questions lie with the rest of the data. I’ve read that unmarked doesn’t have an option for random effects (here from the 4 different sites). But maybe WinBugs does (I’ve never used it)? Or I could run each site separately in unmarked. The other trouble is the different number of passes of pools within a site. Is it possible to include all the data (from an individual site) in the model, even if the numbers of passes are uneven across pools? I tried using all the data lumped together, but came across an error during model specification (“Warning messages: 1: Some observations have been discarded because corresponding covariates were missing) and again when creating a fitList for selection (“Error in validityMethod(object) : Data are not the same among models due to missing covariate values. Consider removing NAs before analysis”). Does this mean that unequal pass numbers within a data set are not allowed?

Is there a better way to take care of the two-diver issue than using diver as a covariate for detection probability?

Any thoughts or suggestions would be much appreciated!

Kristen Kirkby

Graduate Research Assistant
Department of Fisheries and Wildlife
Oregon State University
kristen...@oregonstate.edu

parts:
The only NAs I had in the covariates corresponded to NAs in the y
matrix (in pools where I surveyed fewer than 5 times). I filled in all
the NAs for these covariates with 0s for scaled numeric covariates,
and with one of the two factors already in use for factor variables
(eg. “diver” was either “1” or “2”, NAs were changed to “1”). And this
allowed me to group all my streams together, with stream now included
as a fixed effect.

When I run modSel on a fitlist, it now generates the AIC values, but
it starts that off with the statement that “Hessian is singular”. I
tried to do some digging on that one, but couldn’t quite figure out
whether or not that’s suggesting a problem.

My best model estimates detection probabilities of around 40%, which
is pretty low by coho-counting standards. If I had to make an
educated guess, I’d put it closer to 75%. These pools are small and
clear, often without a ton of obscuring substrates, and coho are not
shy fish, usually hanging out high in the water column. There was a
fairly sizeable difference between the counts of the two snorkelers
(with different experience levels) in most pools, though, so I’m
thinking that’s likely contributing significantly.

This was a “continuous” survey of a stream reach, but only pools were
surveyed, so there was always some stretch of either dry streambed or
flowing riffle between pools. I believe that closure holds pretty well
for these fish. Two of the streams had such low flows that there was
very little or no connectivity between pools. The other two did have
low but continuous flow, so closure becomes a larger assumption there,
but observation and the literature suggest to me that it’s still a
fairly good one.

Andy, you mentioned non-independence as a potential issue, and these
are juvenile coho salmon, so in the bigger pools there’s often some
schooling. I’ll definitely have to look into that.

Thanks very much for the help and suggestions you all offered, I
really appreciate it, and I’m excited to get to know the program
better.

Kristen

messages.subject: RE: [SPAM]  [unmarked] Re: Abundance modeling with uneven pass numbers, two observers
parts:
Hi Kristen,

here's my understanding of your problem. The warning about a singular Hessian in the function modSel appears when at least one model in the set has a singular Hessian. This means that SEs cannot be estimated, or the SEs of some coefficients can't (check out summary() for all the models).

This is no problem for model selection as far as I understand, because you don't need the SEs, but only the deviance and the number of parameters to get the AIC.

Regards -- Marc
